awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Craft Specialization and Economic Organization
awd_abstract_narration:
This doctoral dissertation project investigates the role of craft specialization in shaping social roles and economic relations within village societies. Although the organization and socioeconomic role of craft specialists can vary depending on a society's level of complexity, craft production is integrated into both socioeconomic systems and relationships. Craft specialization can be detected archaeologically through careful examination of household spatial organization, house inventories, and the accumulation of goods. Previous Neolithic research has mainly focused on identifying craft specialization and exchange networks at the site level, whereas, this study focuses on both, as well as the production of items intended for exchange. The project provide scientific training opportunities for students in field methods and artifact analysis.

The research team conducts expansive excavations of Neolithic houses, analyze artifacts, and documents house inventories to determine whether one or more households were involved in tool production, trace their exchange with other villages in the area, and look at the accumulation of goods to look if there are any differences related to craft production, house size, and quantity of goods. The team also examines faunal and botanical remains and investigates any differences in economic modes of subsistence, land ownership, and status within the community. The data collected helps to develop a model for understanding household craft specialization and its implications for village societies.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project investigated how crafts shaped social roles and political economies in village communities during a time marked by increased settlement density and the rise of copper metallurgy in the Central Balkans, especially within the Vinča culture, at the site of Lluga in Kosova.

PhD candidate Zhaneta Gjyshja conducted an eight-week excavation followed by laboratory analysis in 2025 and 2026. The fieldwork involved excavating three units, during which we documented a well-preserved burned-clay house foundation with associated pits, a probable kitchen, a stone-tool workshop, a clay altar, and a palisaded ditch, all dated to the Late Neolithic. We recorded all contexts using drone imagery, drawings, field photography, photogrammetry, and a total station. In the laboratory, we analyzed all stone tools, ceramics, animal bones, and other recovered artifacts, including clay figurines and bone tools. The analysis showed that the structures served different functions and that the site was a stone blade workshop. 

The Late Neolithic Village of Lluga provides a unique, well-dated sequence for the Kosova region and beyond, helping archaeologists understand the use of domestic and non-domestic space in early village communities, the organization of craft production, and broader models of Neolithic economic organization in the Balkans.

The project provided training to ten students from Kosova, six University of Michigan students, one Stanford University student, and four undergraduates from the University of Geneva in Switzerland, and hired local workers to assist with excavation, field documentation, and artifact processing. In addition, we restored multiple ceramic vessels and conserved bone tools and antlers for display in the local museum in the coming years, a goal the project will help achieve. In collaboration with local institutions, we will work to build a small local museum in the village where Lluga is located, where the findings will be displayed and where site visits to the archaeological site will also be possible. 

We maintained our collaboration with the Ministry of Culture and the Archaeological Institute of Kosova. The project made outreach and community engagement efforts by following an open-to-the-public excavation approach that allowed the local community, students, schoolchildren, and other archaeologists in the region to visit, talk with the team, and view the findings. The project also received coverage in multiple local media outlets across Kosova, Albania, and Europe. We submitted the results as a final report to the Archaeological Institute of Kosova in both Albanian and English. They will be included in the dissertation of the student and in a monograph, and all data collected and generated by the project will be published as open source in the Deep Blue repository at the University of Michigan after the dissertation is completed.
